'''Sabine''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|eɪ|b|ɪ|n}} {{respell|SAY|bin}}) is a [[Lunar craters|lunar]] [[impact crater]] that forms a nearly matching pair with [[Ritter (crater)|Ritter]] to the northwest. The two rims are separated by a distance of only a couple of kilometers. To the west is the bowl-shaped crater [[Schmidt (lunar crater)|Schmidt]], and farther to the north are [[Manners (crater)|Manners]] and [[Arago (lunar crater)|Arago]]. Its diameter is 30 km. It was named after Irish physicist and astronomer [[Edward Sabine]].<ref>{{gpn|5258}}</ref>
[[File:Sabine Ritter Schmidt 4085 h1.jpg|thumb|right|[[Lunar Orbiter 4]] image of Sabine (right of center), Ritter (left of center), and Schmidt (lower left) craters]]
[[File:Sabine crater Ritter crater AS16-M-1392.jpg|thumb|right|Oblique view from the south from [[Apollo 16]]]]

==Description==
The outer rim of this crater is roughly circular and relatively featureless. The interior floor has a pair of small craterlets and a central rise. There is a ridge at the western edge of the floor that is concentric with the inner wall.

About 85 km to the east-southeast is 'Statio Tranquillitatis' ([[Tranquility Base]]), the landing site of the [[Apollo 11]] mission and the first human beings to step on the [[Moon]].

[[Ranger 8]] flew over Sabine prior to impact in Mare Tranquilitatis.

Both Sabine and Ritter were originally believed to be [[caldera]]s rather than impact craters.  In ''To A Rocky Moon'', lunar geologist [[Donald Wilhelms|Don E. Wilhelms]] summarized: "They are identical twins in morphology and size (29-30 km).  They lack radial rim [[ejecta]] and [[secondary craters]] despite their apparent youth.  They are positioned at the presumably active edge of a mare.  They are even aligned along [[graben]], the [[Hypatia (crater)|Hypatia]] rilles.  Most significant, they lack deep floors recognized since the days of [[Grove Karl Gilbert|Gilbert]] as diagnostic of impacts."  However, after the Apollo landings were complete, it was realized that "all craters inside basins suffer enhanced [[isostasy|isostatic]] uplift," because "the thin crust and greater heat inside basins lower the [[viscosity]] of the craters' substrate, allowing it to reach isostasy with its surroundings more quickly than can other craters."<ref>To a Rocky Moon: A Geologist's History of Lunar Exploration.  [[Donald Wilhelms|Don E. Wilhelms]], University of Arizona Press (1993). {{ISBN|978-0816510658}}</ref>

==Satellite craters==
By convention these features are identified on lunar maps by placing the letter on the side of the crater midpoint that is closest to Sabine.

The following craters have been renamed by the [[International Astronomical Union|IAU]], after the three astronauts of [[Apollo 11]].<ref>Lunar Chart Series [http://www.lpi.usra.edu/resources/mapcatalog/LAC/lac60/ LAC-60 Julius Caesar], Lunar and Planetary Institute</ref>
* Sabine B — ''See'' [[Aldrin (crater)|Aldrin]].
* Sabine D — ''See'' [[Collins (crater)|Collins]].
* Sabine E — ''See'' [[Armstrong (crater)|Armstrong]].

A crater near the southeast rim of Sabine was referred to as ''Dark Crater'' by the Apollo 11 astronauts.<ref>[https://quickmap.lroc.asu.edu/ LROC QuickMap], nomenclature layer</ref>
